newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh troops find bodies of suspected rebels.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh troops find bodies of suspected rebels.

text.p: Soldiers on routine patrol in dense forests of southeastern Bangladesh found bodies of two suspected tribal rebels on Wednesday, but were unable to say who had shot them.
Police said one of the dead wore a green uniform used by tribal Shanti Bahini guerrillas, who are fighting for autonomy in Chittagong Hill Tracts. The other was in civilian clothes.
The bodies were recovered, along with two guns and few ammunition, early on Tuesday near a border security post in Bandarban, one of three Hill Tract districts.
"Apparently the two were members of the Shanti Bahini and were killed in an exchange of fire between rival groups (of the Shanti Bahini)," one police officer told reporters.
But intelligence sources said the suspected rebels could have been shot by paramilitary troops in a brief shootout with "unidentified attackers around the same place today."
"Also, the victims could be separatist Moslem insurgents from neighbouring Burma using Shanti Bahini's uniform as a disguise," one intelligence officer said.

The 5,500 square-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma, has been the scene of a 24-year insurgency by the Shanti Bahini demanding self-rule and expulsion of some 500,000 Bengali-speaking settlers from the region.
A tough government attitude over the issue of expulsion has dogged peace talks being held in Dhaka with leaders of Shanti Bahini's political wing, official sources said.
"Trying to drive away so many (Bengali) people can lead to a bloody backlash. It's too sensitive an issue," he said.

Other officials said the latest round of talks started on Sunday had been stalled on Tuesday night but might resume after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina returned home on Wednesday from a meeting of South Asian leaders in the Maldives.
The Hill Tracts insurgency has killed more than 8,500 civilians, rebels and securitymen since 1973, according to official figures.
It had also forced some 50,000 tribespeople to flee into northeast India, but over 6,700 returned in March-April as Hasina and the Indian government agreed on a repatriation programme.
Hasina, who took office last June, vowed to find a political settlement to the Hill Tracts problem. But two rounds of peace talks held before the current one have been inconclusive.
